sections.content: This section introduces the core concept of Pāñcarātra philosophy: the Deity's 'modes of being' (prakāras). It explains that early texts like the Sāttvata-saṃhitā and Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā recognize three principal modes: the transcendental (para), the emanatory (vyūha), and the incar-natory (vibhava). Later texts, such as the Śrī-praśna-saṃhitā, expand this to five modes by adding the immanent (antaryāmī or hārda, the inner controller) and the iconic (arcā). The text provides Sanskrit ślokas from Śrī-praśna-saṃhitā and Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā to support this five-fold classification. It clarifies that the transcendental and emanatory forms exist in the high heavens and are directly perceptible only to eternal masters (nitya-sūri) and emancipated souls (mukta). Incarnations (vibhava) are forms on earth seen by their contemporaries, while the inner controller (antaryāmī) is visualized only by sages in meditation. The section concludes by stating that the Pāñcarātra system is fundamentally concerned with enunciating the nature and functions of these modes, and quotes Parāśara-bhaṭṭa who affirms that the three modes (para, vyūha, vibhava) constitute the supreme reality, Brahman.
sections.summary: The section introduces the foundational Pāñcarātra concept of the Deity's modes of being, explaining the evolution from three modes (para, vyūha, vibhava) in early texts to five modes (adding antaryāmī and arcā) in later ones. It defines the nature and accessibility of each of these primary forms.

sections.content: This section details the para, or transcendental mode. The Deity in this state is described as a limitless, profound, and still 'ocean of nectar' (nistaragāmṛtām-bodhi-kalpam), a pure mass of consciousness (cid-ghana) beyond space and time. This transcendental realm is known by various names such as paramam dhāma, śrī-vaikuṇṭha, and parama-vyoma, and is inhabited by eternal masters (nitya-sūris) and emancipated souls (muktas). The Deity is identified as Brahman, whose creative energy (śakti) is indistinguishable from him in this state. This energy is personified as Lakṣmī or Śrī, the inseparable consort of Nārāyaṇa. Lakṣmī is described as movement (kriyā) and the substance of all existence (bhūti). The Deity's initial will to create is termed Su-darśana. The section then introduces the six divine attributes (ṣāḍguṇya) that characterize the Deity: Jñāna (wisdom/consciousness), Śakti (energy), Aiśvarya (lordship), Bala (strength), Vīrya (vigour), and Tejas (splendour). Jñāna is presented as the fundamental attribute upon which the other five depend. These attributes are non-material (aprākṛta), and the term nirguṇa signifies the Deity is untouched by phenomenal qualities. When this creative energy manifests, the Deity is known as Vāsudeva.
sections.summary: This section elaborates on the 'para' (transcendental) mode, describing the Deity as an absolute, formless consciousness in the supreme realm of Vaikuṇṭha. It introduces the inseparable creative energy, Lakṣmī, and details the six fundamental, non-material divine attributes (ṣāḍguṇya) that define this mode, with Jñāna (consciousness) being the foremost.

sections.content: The vyūha mode concerns the differential manifestations and creative configurations of the six divine attributes for the purpose of cosmic evolution and the salvation of devotees. The six attributes are grouped into two functional planes: 'rest' (viśrāma-bhūmayaḥ) comprising jñāna, aiśvarya, and śakti; and 'activity' (śrama-bhūmayaḥ) comprising bala, vīrya, and tejas. The pairing of attributes from these planes results in three vyūha emanations: Saṃkarṣaṇa (Jñāna + Bala), Pradyumna (Aiśvarya + Vīrya), and Aniruddha (Śakti + Tejas). Vāsudeva, who possesses all six attributes in equal measure, is often counted as the fourth vyūha, making a 'catur-vyūha' system. The text distinguishes between Para-Vāsudeva (transcendental, static) and Vyūha-Vāsudeva (dynamic, active). Each of the three vyūhas has specific cosmic functions: Saṃkarṣaṇa supports existence and promulgates scripture; Pradyumna separates puruṣa and prakṛti and provides for spiritual practice; Aniruddha presides over material creation and bestows salvation. However, different texts (Lakṣmī-tantra, Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā, Parama-saṃhitā) assign these creative, preservative, and destructive functions differently among the three. The vyūhas are not separate deities but sequential emanations from Para-Vāsudeva, 'like one lamp lit from another' (dīpād dīpa iva).
sections.summary: This section explains the 'vyūha' (emanatory) mode, where the six divine attributes combine in pairs to form three active emanations—Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha—responsible for cosmic processes and guiding devotees. Along with the source, Vāsudeva, they form the common four-vyūha system. Their specific cosmic functions vary across different Pāñcarātra texts.

sections.content: This section covers the specific manifestations of the Deity, primarily the vibhava (incarnatory) mode. It introduces the concept of the Viśākha-yūpa, a cosmic pillar of light from which the vyūhas emanate as four nodes. This pillar symbolizes Para-Vāsudeva, and the descent from the top node (Vāsudeva) to the bottom (Aniruddha) represents the Deity becoming more accessible. From Aniruddha, the vibhava forms (avatāras or descents) manifest on earth. The text explains that each of the four vyūhas has secondary emanations (vyūhāntara and vidyeśvaras), creating a group of 24 iconic forms. It then lists the ten famous avatāras, associating them with the four vyūhas from which they descend. A distinction is made between direct manifestations (sākṣādavatāra) and forms where the Deity's power possesses a being (āveśāvatāra). A comprehensive list of 38 vibhava forms from the Sāttvata-saṃhitā is provided and described in detail, including figures like Padma-nābha, Ananta, Kapila, Viśva-rūpa, the ten avatāras, and others. The section discusses the classification of these manifestations as primary (mukhya, worship-worthy) or secondary (gauṇa) and notes that different texts classify figures like Buddha and Vyāsa differently. Finally, it integrates the arcā (icon) mode, explaining that it is considered a form of vibhava where divine presence is invoked into a material image through mantras, making the icon a transmuted, non-material form of the Deity.
sections.summary: This section details the 'vibhava' (incarnatory) mode, explaining how specific manifestations (avatāras) descend to earth from the vyūha Aniruddha, as conceptualized through the Viśākha-yūpa model. It provides extensive lists of these manifestations, including the ten primary avatāras and a larger list of 38 forms from the Sāttvata-saṃhitā, and discusses their classification as direct or indirect. The section concludes by incorporating the 'arcā' (icon) as an accessible form of vibhava.

chapter_summary: Chapter V, 'THE DEITY AND ITS MODES', provides a comprehensive analysis of the Pāñcarātra philosophical conception of God. It details the system of the Deity's 'modes of being' (prakāras), which evolved from an early triad—the absolute transcendental (para), the cosmic emanations (vyūha), and earthly incarnations (vibhava)—to a five-fold system including the indwelling controller (antaryāmī) and the worshiped icon (arcā). The chapter meticulously describes each mode. The 'para' mode is the supreme, formless Brahman characterized by six divine attributes (ṣāḍguṇya). The 'vyūha' mode explains how these attributes manifest in combinations as Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha to govern cosmic evolution. The 'vibhava' mode covers the numerous divine descents (avatāras) to earth, providing detailed lists and classifications from various texts. The chapter uses the unifying concept of the 'Viśākha-yūpa' (a cosmic pillar of light) to illustrate the relationships between these modes. It concludes by showing how these abstract theological concepts are made accessible to devotees through worship of the arcā form, which is itself a type of vibhava.
key_arguments: The Pāñcarātra philosophy is uniquely defined by its systematic classification of the Deity into three, four, or five distinct 'modes of being' (prakāras).
The six divine attributes (ṣāḍguṇya: jñāna, śakti, aiśvarya, bala, vīrya, tejas) are foundational to understanding all modes of the Deity, from the unmanifest Para to the active Vyūhas.
The Vyūha emanations (Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha) are not separate deities but functional configurations of the attributes of the one supreme Deity, Vāsudeva, for cosmic purposes.
The Vibhava (incarnations) and Arcā (icons) modes represent the Deity's compassionate descent into the material world, making the divine accessible to devotees.

There is diversity and evolution within Pāñcarātra texts regarding the number of modes, the specific functions of the vyūhas, and the classification of various incarnations, reflecting a rich and dynamic theological tradition.
key_takeaways: The five modes of the Deity in Pāñcarātra are Para (transcendental), Vyūha (emanatory), Vibhava (incarnatory), Antaryāmī (immanent), and Arcā (iconic).
The supreme Deity (Para Vāsudeva) is characterized by six essential attributes: knowledge, energy, lordship, strength, vigour, and splendour.
The four Vyūhas—Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha—are cosmic emanations responsible for creation, preservation, destruction, and salvation.
Vibhavas are the earthly descents (avatāras) of the Deity, which can be direct (sākṣād) or indirect (āveśa).
The Arcā form allows devotees to interact with the Deity directly, as the icon is considered a transmuted divine form, not mere matter.

historical_figures.name: Parāśara-bhaṭṭa
historical_figures.significance: A key commentator on Viṣṇu-sahasra-nāma-stotra whose interpretations on the three modes of the Deity are cited as authoritative.

historical_figures.name: Ālasiṅga-bhaṭṭa
historical_figures.significance: Commentator on the Sāttvata-saṃhitā, whose explanations are referenced, particularly regarding the list of vibhava forms.

historical_figures.name: Otto Schräder
historical_figures.significance: Mentioned for having erroneously identified 39 vibhava forms in the Sāttvata-saṃhitā, a point the author corrects.

historical_figures.name: Brahmā
historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as the four-faced creator produced during the 'mixed creation' phase of Aniruddha. Also personified in the vibhava form Vidyādhideva.

historical_figures.name: Vyāsa
historical_figures.significance: Classified as an 'āveśāvatāra' (divine possession). Also appears as the vibhava form 'Veda-vit', who classified the Vedas.

historical_figures.name: Arjuna
historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as an 'āveśāvatāra' and the recipient of the revelation of the Viśva-rūpa form in Kurkṣetra.

historical_figures.name: Kṛṣṇa
historical_figures.significance: Appears in multiple contexts: as an avatāra from Aniruddha, as 'Pārijāta-hara', and as one of the four ascetic sons of Dharma. His classification as 'sākṣāt' or 'āveśa' is noted as a point of discussion.

historical_figures.name: Rāma
historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as Śrī-rāma, an avatāra who destroyed Rāvaṇa. His classification is also debated.

historical_figures.name: Buddha
historical_figures.significance: Appears as the vibhava form 'Loka-nātha'. His status as a direct or possessed incarnation (sākṣāt vs āveśāvatāra) is shown as a point of difference between texts.

historical_figures.name: Śiva
historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as being empowered to destroy and as part of the composite Dattātreya incarnation.

historical_figures.name: Dattātreya
historical_figures.significance: Listed as a vibhava form, a composite incarnation of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.

geographic_locations.context: The transcendental realm (paramam dhāma), the high heavens where the 'para' mode of the Deity resides.
geographic_locations.significance: It is the ultimate goal for emancipated souls (muktas) and the abode of eternal masters (nitya-sūris).

geographic_locations.context: The battlefield where the Viśva-rūpa (cosmic form) was revealed to Arjuna.
geographic_locations.significance: A key site for a major divine revelation mentioned in the Mahābhārata and Bhagavad-gītā.

geographic_locations.context: A mythical island where the Viśva-rūpa was revealed to Nārada and where the Vihangama (Haṃsa) form abides.
geographic_locations.significance: A sacred place associated with divine manifestations in Pāñcarātra and Puranic literature.

geographic_locations.context: The place where the Dharma-mūrti form of the Deity becomes manifest.
geographic_locations.significance: A sacred forest associated with the personification of Dharma.

geographic_locations.context: The lowest of the netherworlds where Kamatheśvara (Kūrma) abides.
geographic_locations.significance: The cosmic foundation, supported by an incarnation of Viṣṇu.

geographic_locations.context: The celestial garden from which the Pārijāta-flower was snatched by Kṛṣṇa (in his Pārijāta-hara form).
geographic_locations.significance: The setting for a famous mythological episode involving Kṛṣṇa.

geographic_locations.context: The region of Magadha, mentioned in a quote as where the Loka-nātha (Buddha) form is situated.
geographic_locations.significance: Historically associated with the life and teachings of the Buddha.

geographic_locations.context: Mentioned as the location of a crooked mango tree, which is cited as an example of a secondary divine manifestation (gauṇa).
geographic_locations.significance: A location in the Rāmāyaṇa, used here to illustrate the all-pervasiveness of divine intention.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: The principal varieties of forms the Deity assumes in Pāñcarātra philosophy.
The highest, ultimate, and formless mode of the Deity.
The mode of cosmic emanations that govern the universe.
The mode of divine descents or incarnations on earth.
The fourth mode, the inner controller residing in the heart of all beings.
The fifth mode, the form of the Deity worshipped in an icon.
Eternal, ever-free souls residing in Vaikuṇṭha who perpetually see the para form.
Souls who have attained liberation and reside in Vaikuṇṭha.
The six divine qualities that constitute the body of the Deity: jñāna, śakti, aiśvarya, bala, vīrya, tejas.
The primary divine attribute.
A divine attribute; also personified as Lakṣmī.
A divine attribute.
A divine attribute.
A divine attribute.
A divine attribute.
In Pāñcarātra, it means untouched by phenomenal/material (prākṛta) attributes, not the absence of divine attributes.
A manifestation of the Deity on earth, a broader term than vibhava.
A conceptual pillar of light representing Para-Vāsudeva, with nodes for the four vyūhas.
A form where the Deity's nature manifests directly.
A form where the Deity's attributes occasionally possess a divine or human being.

quotations.quote:
मन्मूर्तयः पंचविधा वदन्त्युपनिषत्सु च।
परो व्यूहो हार्द इति विभवोऽर्चेति भेदतः॥
quotations.context: Listing the five modes of the Deity: para, vyūha, hārda (antaryāmī), vibhava, and arcā.

quotations.quote:
मम प्रकाराः पंचेति प्राहुर्वेदान्तपारगाः।
परो व्यूहश्च विभवो नियन्ता सर्वदेहिनाम्।
अर्चावतारश्च तथा दयालुः पुरुषाकृतिः॥
quotations.context: Also listing the five modes, describing the fifth as the compassionate, human-like arcāvatāra.
Defining the Pāñcarātra system as that which expounds the nature of the para, vyūha, and vibhava modes.
Stating that the supreme Brahman is three-fold as para, vyūha, and vibhava, which is the doctrine of the Bhāgavatas.
Describing how the eternal and liberated souls directly see the supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa.

quotations.quote:
षाड्गुण्यविग्रहं देवं भास्वज्ज्वलनतेजसम्।
सर्वतः पाणिपादं तत् सर्वतोऽक्षिशिरोमुखम्।
परमेतत् समाख्यातं सर्वाश्रयं प्रभुम्॥
quotations.context: Describing the transcendental mode of the Deity as having a body of the six divine attributes.

quotations.quote:
अजडं स्वात्मसम्बेधि नित्यं सर्वावगाहनम्।
ज्ञानं नाम गुणं प्राहुः प्रथमं गुणचिन्तकाः॥
quotations.context: Defining Jñāna (wisdom) as the first and foremost of the divine attributes.

quotations.quote:
शक्तेः शक्तिमतो भेदाद्वासुदेव इतीर्यते।
सर्वशक्तिमयो देवो वासुदेवः सिसृक्षया॥
quotations.context: Explaining that Vāsudeva is the name given to the Deity when Śakti (energy) differentiates for the sake of creation.

quotations.quote:
एतत्पूर्वं त्रयं चान्यत् ज्ञानाद्यैर्भेदितं गुणैः।
विद्धि तद् व्यूहसंज्ञं तन्निः श्रेयसफलप्रदम्।
quotations.context: Stating that after the first (Vāsudeva), the other three forms, differentiated by attributes like Jñāna, are known as Vyūhas.
Explaining that the manifest forms are non-different from the original form, just as a tree is contained within its seed.

tables_and_charts.description: A structured list showing the three Vyūha emanations as pairings of the six divine attributes.
tables_and_charts.data_summary:
(1) jñāna + bala -> Saṃkarṣaṇa
(2) aiśvarya + vīrya -> Pradyumna
(3) śakti + tejas -> Aniruddha

tables_and_charts.description: A comprehensive list of the 24 forms (caturviṃśati-mūrti-gaṇa) organized under the four main Vyūhas, each subdivided into three Vyūhāntaras and three Vidyeśvaras.
tables_and_charts.data_summary:
I. Vyūha-Vāsudeva: Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava; Vāsudeva, Puruṣottama, Janārdana.
II. Vyūha-Saṃkarṣaṇa: Govinda, Viṣṇu, Madhusūdana; Saṃkarṣaṇa, Adhokṣaja, Upendra.
III. Vyūha-Pradyumna: Trivikrama, Vāmana, Śrīdhara; Pradyumna, Nṛsiṃha, Hari.
IV. Vyūha-Aniruddha: Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, Dāmodara; Aniruddha, Acyuta, Kṛṣṇa.

tables_and_charts.description: A list of the ten well-known avatāras, categorized according to the Vyūha form from which they are said to descend, based on Pādma-tantra.
tables_and_charts.data_summary:
I. From Vāsudeva: Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha
II. From Saṃkarṣaṇa: Nṛsiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma, Paraśurāma
III. From Pradyumna: Bala-rāma
IV. From Aniruddha: Kṛṣṇa, Kalkin

tables_and_charts.description: An enumerated list of 38 vibhava (incarnatory) forms according to the Sāttvata-saṃhitā.
tables_and_charts.data_summary: The list begins with Padma-nābha, Dhruva, Ananta and continues through all major and minor incarnations including Kapila, Viśva-rūpa, the ten primary avatāras, Dattātreya, Nara-Nārāyaṇa, and concludes with Pātāla-śayana.

footnotes_endnotes.content: The final quotation on page 37 is attributed to 'the commentary on Sāttvata-saṃhitā, 1,27, ed. by Vraja-Vallabha Dvivedi, Vārāṇasi, 1982, p.9'. This commentary is by Parāśara-bhaṭṭa.

controversial_points: The assignment of cosmic functions (creation, preservation, dissolution) to the three vyūhas (Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha) differs across texts like Lakṣmī-tantra, Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā, and Parama-saṃhitā.

The classification of certain avatāras, particularly Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and Vyāsa, varies between being direct manifestations (sākṣāt) and divine possessions (āveśa) depending on the source text (e.g., Tattva-traya vs. Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā vs. Parāśara-bhaṭṭa).

The author points out an error made by the scholar Otto Schräder in counting the number of vibhava forms in the Sāttvata-saṃhitā, clarifying that 'Śāntātmā' is an epithet for 'Loka-nātha' (Buddha) and not a separate form.

alternative_viewpoints.description: Some texts like Sāttvata-saṃhitā speak of three vyūhas (Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha) emanating from the transcendental Vāsudeva. However, the more common view recognizes four vyūhas, counting Vāsudeva as the first among them.

A distinction is made in some texts between Para-Vāsudeva (transcendental, inactive) and Vyūha-Vāsudeva (dynamic, involved in creation). Other texts propose a further distinction of a formless Parātpara-Vāsudeva.
While the general theory is that all manifestations emerge from Aniruddha, the Pādma-tantra presents a scheme where different avatāras descend from all four of the vyūhas.
